name: Decision Flowchart
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Decision Flowchart: One Path Through Everything You've Learned
lesson.summary: This chapter compresses the decision framework and the when-not-to-use-blockchain checklist into a single sequential flowchart with hard stop gates, then walks a realistic cold-chain scenario through it step by step to show how the reasoning plays out in practice.
lesson.body:
Every decision framework you've built so far in this course, the weighted criteria scorecard, the when-not-to-use-blockchain checklist, the cost-benefit comparisons, has the same weakness: none of it forces you to look at the criteria in a fixed order. A scorecard can be gamed. If someone in the room already wants blockchain, whether because a vendor pitched it well, because a competitor announced a pilot, or because it is genuinely more interesting to build than a database migration, a scorecard gives them room to weight the criteria that favor their answer more heavily and wave off the ones that don't. A flowchart with hard sequential gates closes that room. You cannot reach gate four without having honestly answered gates one through three, and a no anywhere ends the conversation immediately, before anyone has invested more effort defending a conclusion they arrived at emotionally.

That is the actual purpose of turning two chapters' worth of criteria into one flowchart: not to teach you anything new about blockchain, but to teach you a discipline for applying what you already know under organizational pressure, where cognitive biases like novelty bias (new technology feels like progress even when it solves nothing new) and sunk cost (three months of vendor meetings makes no feel wasteful) push hardest.

Here is the flowchart, compressed into six gates that follow directly from the decision framework and the when-not-to-use-blockchain checklist. Gate one asks whether the data even needs to be shared across organizational boundaries. If it is purely internal record keeping, stop, you need a database, not a blockchain, because there is no multi-party trust problem to solve. Gate two asks whether more than one organization needs to write to the shared record, not just read it. Plenty of legitimate cross-company data sharing is one writer and many readers, a manufacturer publishing signed certificates that retailers verify, for example. A single writer with many readers is solved by publishing signed data from a regular server. Blockchain earns its keep only when multiple mutually independent parties need to write.

Gate three asks whether those writers already trust a common intermediary to operate a shared database honestly. If a bank, a regulator, or an industry consortium everyone already trusts is willing to run the system, a centrally operated shared database is cheaper, faster, and easier to change than a blockchain, and it solves the same coordination problem. Gate four asks whether you need the history of that shared record to be tamper evident, specifically resistant to any single party or small coalition quietly rewriting the past, beyond what access controlled logging and offsite backups already provide. Many organizations that think they need immutability actually need better audit logging, which is a much smaller project.

Gate five asks whether the parties involved can live with blockchain's actual performance profile: transaction latency measured in seconds or longer depending on the network, finite throughput, and the practical impossibility of quietly deleting or correcting a bad record once it is confirmed, which cuts against data protection rules that grant a right to erasure. Gate six is the final cost-benefit gate: does the value of solving a genuine multi-writer, low-trust, tamper-evidence problem outweigh the operational complexity of running or joining a distributed system, including governance overhead, key management, and node operations, compared with the next best alternative?

Walk this through with a realistic case. Meridian Foods is a coalition of regional produce growers, a refrigerated logistics carrier, and three grocery retailers who jointly need to prove that leafy greens never left an acceptable temperature range between farm and shelf, because one contamination scare tied to a broken cold chain can trigger a recall across every retailer that carried that batch, and regulators are asking for auditable proof, not just paperwork.

Gate one: does the data cross organizational boundaries? Yes, temperature readings are captured by the carrier's refrigerated trucks, but growers and retailers both need to see and rely on them. Gate two: is there more than one writer? Yes, the carrier logs in-transit temperature, the growers log harvest conditions, and each retailer logs receiving-dock temperature at handoff, three independent organizations writing to the same record. Gate three: do they trust a common intermediary? This is where most teams get lazy and assume the answer is obviously no. It is worth testing seriously: could a neutral third-party auditor or an industry cooperative run a shared database that all four parties trust equally? In Meridian's case, no existing party has that trust, the carrier has been caught rounding temperature logs favorably before, and no retailer wants a competitor's preferred vendor holding the master copy. So the answer genuinely is no, proceed.

Gate four: is tamper evidence worth more than better logging? Yes, because the whole point is that no single party, including the carrier who has an incentive to hide a cold chain break, can quietly edit their own past entries after a recall investigation starts. Gate five: can they tolerate blockchain's performance and immutability tradeoffs? Temperature logging is not latency sensitive, a reading confirmed within a minute is fine, and nothing here needs to be erased later, so yes. Gate six: does the benefit outweigh the complexity? Given that a single recall event can cost far more than the cost of running four to six validator nodes among the consortium members, and the alternative of mutual audits and trust-based paperwork has already failed to satisfy regulators, yes.

Meridian clears all six gates, which tells you two things at once: blockchain is justified here, and specifically a permissioned network among the known consortium members is justified, not a public blockchain, since gate three's answer was about trusting each other, not about trusting an unknown, permissionless validator set. Notice that the flowchart didn't just produce a yes, it produced a shape: multi-writer, permissioned, optimized for tamper evidence over throughput. That shape is exactly what feeds into the implementation roadmap and the architecture report later in this arc. A flowchart that only outputs yes or no isn't finished doing its job; a good one hands you the starting sketch of the system you're about to design.
